questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: Hihi

Stitchbird / hihi (Notiomystis cincta) are medium-sized honeyeaters endemic to the North Island of New Zealand. They inhabit mature podocarp-broadleaf forests and are valued as a taonga species by many iwi.

Fossil evidence and genetic studies indicate that hihi were once widespread throughout both islands. During the Pleistocene glaciations (approximately 2.5 million – 11,700 years ago), advancing ice sheets and cooling climates fragmented forest habitats, isolating hihi populations in separate glacial refugia in the Northland, Coromandel, and central North Island regions.

As forests recovered after the last glaciation, some populations expanded, but many remained separated by farmland and deforested areas. The introduction of rats, possums, and stoats caused a dramatic population decline. Today hihi survive in only a few managed mainland reserves and on one predator-free island where a small group was translocated.

Genetic analysis of microsatellite markers reveals distinct genetic clusters corresponding to the glacial refugia. The island population established from a small translocated group shows markedly lower genetic diversity than its mainland source population, with some alleles becoming fixed.

Discuss factors affecting the evolution of hihi. In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms founder population and gene flow
- how the Pleistocene glaciations may have contributed to divergent evolution by allopatric speciation
- why translocating hihi between island and mainland populations could prevent further speciation.
questions.expectedAnswer: Describe founder population (a small group that colonises a new area with only a subset of the original gene pool), gene flow (movement of alleles between populations), allopatric speciation (geographic isolation leading to genetic divergence), divergent evolution (related populations becoming increasingly different due to different selection pressures).

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Patterns of evolution in gecko

New Zealand has a remarkably diverse gecko fauna, with over 45 endemic species across several genera. Many of these species are found in specific geographic regions and occupy distinct ecological niches — some are arboreal specialists living in forest canopy, while others inhabit lowland forests or rocky shorelines.

On the Three Kings Islands, 55 km north-west of mainland New Zealand, several endemic giant gecko species are found. These Three Kings species are closely related to different mainland species, suggesting separate colonisation events rather than a single ancestor diversifying on the islands.

Phylogenetic analysis shows that the diversification of gecko in New Zealand occurred in bursts, particularly during periods of mountain building and glaciation that created new habitats and barriers.

Discuss factors of the evolution of gecko in New Zealand and the Three Kings Islands.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms allopatric and species, including definitions
- the rate of evolution shown in the phylogeny, identifying whether it best represents gradualism or punctuated equilibrium
- why adaptive radiation is more extensive among mainland New Zealand gecko than among Three Kings Island gecko
- TWO reproductive isolating mechanisms (RIMs) that may prevent hybridisation between closely related gecko species that now overlap in range.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define species (individuals that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring) and allopatric (populations separated by a geographic barrier). Punctuated equilibrium best explains bursts of diversification during tectonic/glacial events.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Convergent evolution in aquatic insectivores

Aquatic insect-hunting has evolved independently in several unrelated bird lineages around the world. The pīwauwau / rock wren (Xenicus gilviventris) of New Zealand and the white-throated dipper (Cinclus cinclus) of Europe are not closely related — their common ancestor lived over 65 million years ago — yet they share remarkably similar adaptations:
- streamlined body for swimming in fast-flowing rivers
- strong, gripping feet for walking on slippery rocks
- dense, waterproof plumage
- reduced wing area for underwater manoeuvring
- specialised bill shape for scraping invertebrates from rocks

Despite these similarities, the pīwauwau has a distinctive fleshy lip on its bill for filtering invertebrates, while the dipper lacks this feature and instead bobs underwater to catch prey. Their foraging techniques also differ: the pīwauwau filters while swimming on the surface, while the dipper walks along the riverbed.

Discuss how convergent evolution is linked to selection pressures.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- selection pressures, including descriptions with examples
- how genetic data is used to show convergent evolution
- how the process of natural selection has resulted in analogous structures.
questions.expectedAnswer: Describe selection pressures (environmental factors influencing survival and reproduction), convergent evolution (unrelated species developing similar traits in similar environments), natural selection, analogous features (similar function but different structure/origin).
